description: 🚀 The Orbiters is a team passionate about space exploration and innovation. For the Space Mission Design Game challenge, we aim to create an interactive gaming experience where players can design space missions, explore planets, manage resources, and make strategic decisions. 🪐 Combining science, coding, AI, and storytelling, we want to make space exploration fun and educational. 🌌 नई सोच, नई उड़ान, अनंत ब्रह्मांड! ✨
summary:
Every real space mission begins with a blank page and a hard question: what do we want to learn, and what will it cost to find out? MISSION ZERO puts that question in your hands.

In this browser game, you become a mission architect. You pick a need, like watching weather from space or bringing internet to remote places. Then you build the spacecraft part by part, choose an orbit and a rocket, and set up the ground stations that bring the data home. Six live meters (budget, mass, power, data, communications and mission lifetime) move with every choice, so the trade-offs are impossible to miss. Spacecraft too heavy for the rocket? The launch is blocked.

Then comes launch day. The game runs your mission and explains, in plain language, why it succeeded or fell short, and matches your design to a real NASA science mission.

It is built around NASA’s four mission segments, its six-step design process and its Concept Maturity Levels, using simplified game values rather than real mission data. We made it so that beginners can feel how space missions are designed, not just read about it.
details:
The idea. Real space missions don’t start with a rocket. They start with a question: what do we need to know, and what will it take to find out? MISSION ZERO hands that question to the player. You become the mission architect, and you find out whether your design actually works.

What it does. You pick a scenario (Weather Watch, Rural Internet or Moon Orbiter) and a difficulty (Cadet, Engineer or Director). A mission brief lays out the need, the goals and the measurable requirements. Then you build: a spacecraft from its bus, solar panels, battery, radio, computer, pointing system, propulsion and science instruments; an orbit and a rocket; and the ground stations that bring data home. Six meters stay on screen the whole time: budget (in rupees, crore), mass, power, data, communications and mission lifetime. Every choice moves them, so the trade-offs show up immediately.

How it works. When you launch, a simulation engine totals mass, power, data, cost and lifetime. It checks that the rocket can lift your spacecraft to your orbit, and if it can’t, the launch is blocked. It compares the data you produce with the data your ground stations can receive, then tests every requirement. The results screen gives a score, shows what passed or failed, and explains why in plain language. For example, it tells you when science data was lost because the down link was too small. It also shows a concept-maturity checklist and matches your design to a real NASA science mission.

Built on a real approach. The game follows NASA’s four mission segments (launch, space, ground, user) and its six-step design process, shown as a progress tracker. The checklist is inspired by NASA’s Concept Maturity Levels: the game uses levels 1 to 4, and a level counts as reached at 80% completion. Margin targets reward designs that keep spare capacity. Small-spacecraft classes and the 10% budget reserve draw on CubeSat guidance. The game uses NASA’s published methods and public mission information as reference, not live data feeds.

Why it matters. More instruments mean more science, but also more mass, power, cost and data. There is rarely one perfect answer, so players experiment and learn from the explanations. Four advisers (Mission Planner, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, and Comms and Ground) give live advice and sometimes disagree, as real teams do. Tooltips and a short tutorial keep it open to beginners, so it suits students, classrooms and anyone curious about systems engineering.

Creativity. A dark, cinematic mission-control interface sits over one continuous 3D scene (Earth, orbit rings, satellite) whose camera moves between steps. All of it is generated in code, with no downloaded images or textures. Resource bars are segmented, and “why this happened” cards replace a bare pass or fail.

What we considered. Clarity for beginners, honest numbers, accessibility (keyboard use, reduced motion, text alongside color), and no NASA branding. All values are simplified game numbers, not real mission data. Online multiplayer is future work; for now the four advisers stand in for a team.

Tools. React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Three.js.

AI disclosure. MISSION ZERO was developed with AI assistance. The game code, interface and 3D scene were generated and refined with Google AI Studio and Claude, and reviewed, tested and integrated by the team. Text generated with AI assistance and reviewed, refined, and edited by Team The Orbiters.
